title: They didn’t die in rebellion.
paragraphs:
They didn’t die in rebellion.
They died in worship.
Let that sit.

Because that means it’s possible to be close to God…
and still be completely out of line with Him.

Two men.
Chosen.
Anointed.
Standing in the presence of glory.

And in one moment—
fire fell.

Not the kind that blesses.
The kind that consumes.
Why?
What did they do that was so serious… that God responded with fire?
Here’s the tension most people don’t want to face:

They weren’t atheists.
They weren’t idol worshipers.
They weren’t outside the system.

They were inside.
Serving.
Leading.
Wearing the garments.

And still—
they offered something God never asked for.

“Nadab and Abihu… offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which He had not commanded them. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them…”
— Leviticus 10:1–2
Catch that phrase.
“Which He had not commanded them.”
That’s the whole issue.

Not just what they did—
but that God never asked for it.
This is where it gets uncomfortably personal.

Because today, we don’t carry censers and incense—
but we still bring God things He never asked for.

Performance instead of purity.
Emotion instead of obedience.
Noise instead of surrender.

We raise hands… but resist His Word.
We sing loud… but live quiet rebellion.
We serve publicly… but hide privately.
And we call it worship.

But heaven is not moved by what feels spiritual.
Heaven responds to what is obedient.

Some scholars interpret that Nadab and Abihu may have used the wrong source of fire—
not the fire from the altar God had ignited (Leviticus 9:24),
but something man-made.
That detail matters.
Because it reveals something deeper:
They replaced God’s fire with their own.
And God would not accept it.
Pause.

How much of what we offer today…
is powered by our own fire?

Our ideas.
Our timing.
Our preferences.
Our platform.

Instead of:
“Lord, what have You commanded?”
This is the danger of familiarity.

They had seen glory before.
They had been in holy spaces.

And somewhere along the way—
holy became common.

And when holy becomes common…
obedience becomes optional.
But God responds:

“Among those who are near Me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.”
— Leviticus 10:3
God is not adjusting Himself to us.
We are called to align with Him.
This is not about fear-based religion.
This is about rightly seeing God.

Holy.
Pure.
Set apart.
Not to be approached casually.
And here’s the part that hits hardest:
You can be active in ministry… and still be offering strange fire.

You can preach—
and still not obey.

You can lead—
and still not surrender.

You can be seen as spiritual—
and still be out of alignment with God.
That realization brings shame.
The quiet kind.
The kind that whispers:

“Have I been doing this wrong?”
“Is my worship real?”
“Have I been offering God… something He never asked for?”
Stay with me.
Because this is where everything turns.
The story of Nadab and Abihu is not just a warning.
It’s a signpost pointing forward.

Because if approaching a holy God requires perfect obedience—
then who can stand?

Not Nadab.
Not Abihu.
Not you.
Not me.
That’s why we need Jesus.

“For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses… yet without sin.”
— Hebrews 4:15
Jesus never offered strange fire.
Not once.

Every step.
Every word.
Every act.
Perfect obedience.

“I always do the things that are pleasing to Him.”
— John 8:29

Where Nadab and Abihu failed—
Jesus fulfilled.
And then…
He did something scandalous.
He didn’t just live perfectly.
He died in our place.

“Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that He might bring us to God…”
— 1 Peter 3:18
Let that land.

The fire that should have consumed us—
fell on Him.

The judgment we deserved—
He absorbed.
So now…
We don’t come to God with our own fire.
We come through Christ.

“Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace…”
— Hebrews 4:16
Not confidence in ourselves.
Confidence in Jesus.
This is the shift:

From strange fire
to saving grace

From
“Look what I brought”
to
“Jesus, I need what You’ve done.”
So what do we do now?
We repent.

Not just of obvious sin—
but of self-made worship.

We lay down the need to control.
To impress.
To perform.
And we ask:
“Lord… what have You commanded?”
Because true worship is not built on creativity alone.
It is built on obedience to God’s Word.

“God is spirit, and those who worship Him must worship in spirit and truth.”
— John 4:24
Truth matters.
His way matters.
Right now—this is personal.
Not theoretical.
What are you offering God… that He never asked for?
What needs to be surrendered?
What needs to be realigned?
You are not too far gone.
You are not disqualified.
You are not beyond grace.
But you must come the right way.
Through Jesus.
If this is you—don’t ignore it.
This is not guilt.
This is God calling you back.
Say it.
Mean it.
Let it be real:
“Jesus, I surrender my way. Teach me Yours.”
If this woke you up…
From strange fire to saving grace — because Jesus rewrites everything.
